items.title: Milky Way over Yellowstone
items.summary: The Milky Way was not created by an evaporating lake. The colorful pool of water, about 10 meters across, is known as Silex Spring and is located in Yellowstone National Park in Wyoming, USA. Illuminated artificially, the colors are caused by layers of bacteria that grow in the hot spring. Steam rises off the spring, heated by underground magma associated with the Yellowstone Hotspot. items.source: Book I, chapter 1 · trans. James Legge

items.summary: When you know a thing, to hold that you know it; and when you do not know a thing, to allow that you do not know it;—this is knowledge.
items.source: Book II, chapter 17 · trans. James Legge

items.label: From the classics
items.title: Confucius — The Analects
items.summary: The superior man is modest in his speech, but exceeds in his actions.
items.source: Book XIV, chapter 29 · trans. James Legge

items.source: Book XV, chapter 23 · trans. James Legge

items.label: From the classics
items.title: Laozi — Tao Teh King
items.summary: The highest excellence is like that of water. The excellence of water appears in its benefiting all things, and in its occupying, without striving, the low place which all men dislike.

items.label: From the classics
items.title: Laozi — Tao Teh King
items.summary: Who can make the muddy water clear? Let it be still, and it will gradually become clear.

items.label: From the classics
items.title: Laozi — Tao Teh King
items.summary: He who knows other men is discerning; he who knows himself is intelligent. He who overcomes others is strong; he who overcomes himself is mighty.

items.label: From the classics
items.title: Laozi — Tao Teh King
items.summary: All difficult things in the world are sure to arise from a previous state in which they were easy, and all great things from one in which they were small.

items.label: From the classics
items.title: The Dhammapada
items.summary: For hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love, this is an old rule.

items.label: From the classics
items.title: The Dhammapada
items.summary: By rousing himself, by earnestness, by restraint and control, the wise man may make for himself an island which no flood can overwhelm.

items.label: From the classics
items.title: The Dhammapada
items.summary: As the bee collects nectar and departs without injuring the flower, or its colour or scent, so let a sage dwell in his village.

items.label: From the classics
items.title: The Dhammapada
items.summary: Let no man think lightly of good. Even by the falling of water-drops a water-pot is filled; the wise man becomes full of good, even if he gather it little by little.

items.label: From the classics
items.title: The Bhagavad-Gita — The Song Celestial
items.summary: Find full reward of doing right in right! Let right deeds be thy motive, not the fruit which comes from them.
items.source: Chapter II · trans. Sir Edwin Arnold

items.label: From the classics

items.summary: In sorrows not dejected, and in joys not overjoyed; dwelling outside the stress of passion, fear, and anger; fixed in calms of lofty contemplation.
items.source: Chapter II · trans. Sir Edwin Arnold

items.label: From the classics
items.title: The Bhagavad-Gita — The Song Celestial
items.summary: Let each man raise the Self by Soul, not trample down his Self, since Soul that is Self's friend may grow Self's foe.
items.source: Chapter VI · trans. Sir Edwin Arnold

items.label: From the classics
items.title: The Bhagavad-Gita — The Song Celestial
items.summary: Steadfast a lamp burns sheltered from the wind; such is the likeness of the Yogi's mind shut from sense-storms and burning bright to Heaven.
items.source: Chapter VI · trans. Sir Edwin Arnold

items.label: From the classics
items.title: Plato — Apology
items.summary: A man who is good for anything ought not to calculate the chance of living or dying; he ought only to consider whether in doing anything he is doing right or wrong.

items.label: From the classics
items.title: Plato — Apology
items.summary: For the fear of death is indeed the pretence of wisdom, and not real wisdom, being a pretence of knowing the unknown.

items.label: From the classics
items.title: Plato — Apology
items.summary: I do nothing but go about persuading you all, old and young alike, not to take thought for your persons or your properties, but first and chiefly to care about the greatest improvement of the soul.

items.label: From the classics
items.title: Plato — Apology
items.summary: The unexamined life is not worth living.

items.label: From the classics
items.title: Plato — Apology
items.summary: Be of good cheer about death, and know of a certainty, that no evil can happen to a good man, either in life or after death.

items.label: From the classics
items.title: Mary Wollstonecraft — A Vindication of the Rights of Woman
items.summary: Strengthen the female mind by enlarging it, and there will be an end to blind obedience.

items.label: From the classics
items.title: Mary Wollstonecraft — A Vindication of the Rights of Woman
items.summary: Let their faculties have room to unfold, and their virtues to gain strength, and then determine where the whole sex must stand in the intellectual scale.

items.label: From the classics
items.title: Mary Wollstonecraft — A Vindication of the Rights of Woman
items.summary: How can a rational being be ennobled by any thing that is not obtained by its own exertions?

items.label: From the classics
items.title: Mary Wollstonecraft — A Vindication of the Rights of Woman
items.summary: Let us endeavour to strengthen our minds by reflection, till our heads become a balance for our hearts.

items.label: From the classics
items.title: Mary Wollstonecraft — A Vindication of the Rights of Woman
items.summary: Rights and duties are inseparable.

items.summary: The only freedom which deserves the name, is that of pursuing our own good in our own way, so long as we do not attempt to deprive others of theirs, or impede their efforts to obtain it.

items.label: From the classics
items.title: John Stuart Mill — On Liberty
items.summary: The peculiar evil of silencing the expression of an opinion is, that it is robbing the human race; posterity as well as the existing generation.

items.label: From the classics
items.title: John Stuart Mill — On Liberty
items.summary: If wrong, they lose, what is almost as great a benefit, the clearer perception and livelier impression of truth, produced by its collision with error.

items.label: From the classics
items.title: John Stuart Mill — On Liberty
items.summary: As it is useful that while mankind are imperfect there should be different opinions, so is it that there should be different experiments of living.

items.label: Poem
items.title: Homer — The Iliad
items.summary:
Achilles’ wrath, to Greece the direful spring
Of woes unnumber’d, heavenly goddess, sing!
That wrath which hurl’d to Pluto’s gloomy reign
The souls of mighty chiefs untimely slain;
items.source: Book I, opening · trans. Alexander Pope · Project Gutenberg

items.label: Poem
items.title: Homer — The Iliad
items.summary:
Now pleasing sleep had seal’d each mortal eye,
Stretch’d in the tents the Grecian leaders lie:
The immortals slumber’d on their thrones above;
All, but the ever-wakeful eyes of Jove.
items.source: Book II · trans. Alexander Pope · Project Gutenberg

items.label: Poem
items.title: Homer — The Iliad
items.summary:
Thus having said, the glorious chief resumes
His towery helmet, black with shading plumes.
His princess parts with a prophetic sigh,
Unwilling parts, and oft reverts her eye
That stream’d at every look; then, moving slow,
Sought her own palace, and indulged her woe.
items.source: Book VI · trans. Alexander Pope · Project Gutenberg

items.label: Poem
items.title: Homer — The Iliad
items.source: Book XVIII, the shield of Achilles · trans. Alexander Pope · Project Gutenberg

items.label: Poem
items.title: Homer — The Iliad
items.summary:
’Twas when, emerging through the shades of night,
The morning planet told the approach of light;
And, fast behind, Aurora’s warmer ray
O’er the broad ocean pour’d the golden day:
items.source: Book XXIII · trans. Alexander Pope · Project Gutenberg

items.label: Poem
items.title: Homer — The Iliad
items.summary:
Fear not thy rivals, though for swiftness known;
Compare those rivals’ judgment and thy own:
It is not strength, but art, obtains the prize,
And to be swift is less than to be wise.
items.source: Book XXIII · trans. Alexander Pope · Project Gutenberg

items.label: Poem
items.title: Homer — The Iliad
items.summary:
Rise, then: let reason mitigate your care:
To mourn avails not: man is born to bear.
Such is, alas! the gods’ severe decree:
They, only they are blest, and only free.
items.source: Book XXIV · trans. Alexander Pope · Project Gutenberg

items.label: Poem
items.title: Homer — The Odyssey
items.summary:
The man for wisdom’s various arts renown’d,
Long exercised in woes, O Muse! resound;
Who, when his arms had wrought the destined fall
Of sacred Troy, and razed her heaven-built wall,
Wandering from clime to clime, observant stray’d,
Their manners noted, and their states survey’d,
items.source: Book I, opening · trans. Alexander Pope · Project Gutenberg

items.label: Poem
items.title: Homer — The Odyssey
items.summary:
Ulysses’ son: but happier he, whom fate
Hath placed beneath the storms which toss the great!
Happier the son, whose hoary sire is bless’d
With humble affluence, and domestic rest!
Happier than I, to future empire born,
But doom’d a father’s wretch’d fate to mourn!
items.source: Book I · trans. Alexander Pope · Project Gutenberg

items.label: Poem
items.title: Homer — The Odyssey
items.summary:
The counsel of my friend (the youth rejoin’d)
Imprints conviction on my grateful mind.
So fathers speak (persuasive speech and mild)
Their sage experience to the favourite child.
items.source: Book I · trans. Alexander Pope · Project Gutenberg

items.label: Poem
items.title: Homer — The Odyssey
items.summary:
O prince, in early youth divinely wise,
Born, the Ulysses of thy age to rise
If to the son the father’s worth descends,
O’er the wide wave success thy ways attends
To tread the walks of death he stood prepared;
And what he greatly thought, he nobly dared.
items.source: Book II · trans. Alexander Pope · Project Gutenberg

items.label: Poem
items.title: Homer — The Odyssey
items.summary:
Elysium shall be thine: the blissful plains
Of utmost earth, where Rhadamanthus reigns.
Joys ever young, unmix’d with pain or fear,
Fill the wide circle of the eternal year:
Stern winter smiles on that auspicious clime:
The fields are florid with unfading prime;
items.source: Book IV · trans. Alexander Pope · Project Gutenberg

items.label: Poem
items.title: Homer — The Odyssey
items.summary:
Nine prosperous days we plied the labouring oar;
The tenth presents our welcome native shore:
The hills display the beacon’s friendly light,
And rising mountains gain upon our sight.
Then first my eyes, by watchful toils oppress’d,
Complied to take the balmy gifts of rest:
items.source: Book X · trans. Alexander Pope · Project Gutenberg

items.label: Poem
items.title: William Blake — The Lily
items.summary:
The modest Rose puts forth a thorn,
The humble sheep a threat’ning horn:
While the Lily white shall in love delight,
Nor a thorn nor a threat stain her beauty bright.

items.label: Poem
items.title: Emily Dickinson — A Word
items.summary:
A word is dead
When it is said,
Some say.
I say it just
Begins to live
That day.
items.source: Complete poem · Third Series, Life VI · Project Gutenberg

items.label: Poem
items.title: חיים נחמן ביאליק — הכניסיני תחת כנפך
items.summary:
הַכְנִיסִינִי תַּחַת כְּנָפֵךְ,
וַהֲיִי לִי אֵם וְאָחוֹת,
וִיהִי חֵיקֵךְ מִקְלַט רֹאשִׁי,
קַן־תְּפִלּוֹתַי הַנִּדָּחוֹת.

items.label: Poem
items.title: חיים נחמן ביאליק — הכניסיני תחת כנפך
items.summary:
וּבְעֵת רַחֲמִים, בֵּין־הַשְּׁמָשׁוֹת,
שְׁחִי וַאֲגַל לָךְ סוֹד יִסּוּרָי:
אוֹמְרִים, יֵשׁ בָּעוֹלָם נְעוּרִים –
הֵיכָן נְעוּרָי?

items.label: Poem
items.title: חיים נחמן ביאליק — הכניסיני תחת כנפך
items.summary:
וְעוֹד רָז אֶחָד לָךְ אֶתְוַדֶּה:
נַפְשִׁי נִשְׂרְפָה בְלַהֲבָהּ;
אוֹמְרִים, אַהֲבָה יֵשׁ בָּעוֹלָם –
מַה־זֹּאת אַהֲבָה?

items.label: Poem
items.title: חיים נחמן ביאליק — הכניסיני תחת כנפך
items.summary:
הַכּוֹכָבִים רִמּוּ אוֹתִי,
הָיָה חֲלוֹם – אַךְ גַּם הוּא עָבָר;
עַתָּה אֵין לִי כְלוּם בָּעוֹלָם –
אֵין לִי דָבָר.

items.label: Poem
items.title: רחל בלובשטיין — רק על עצמי
items.summary:
רַק עַל עַצְמִי לְסַפֵּר יָדַעְתִּי
צַר עוֹלָמִי כְּעוֹלַם נְמָלָה,
גַּם מַשָּׂאִי עָמַסְתִּי כָּמוֹהָ
רַב וְכָבֵד מִכְּתֵפִי הַדַּלָּה.

items.label: Poem
items.title: רחל בלובשטיין — רק על עצמי
items.summary:
גַּם אֶת דַּרְכִּי – כְּדַרְכָּהּ אֶל צַמֶּרֶת –
דֶּרֶך מַכְאוֹב וְדֶרֶךְ עָמָל,
יַד עֲנָקִים זְדוֹנָה וּבוֹטַחַת,
יַד מִתְבַּדַּחַת שָׂמָה לְאַל.

items.label: Poem
items.title: רחל בלובשטיין — רק על עצמי
items.summary:
כָּל אָרְחוֹתַי הִלִּיז וְהִדְמִיע
פַּחַד טָמִיר מִיַּד עֲנָקִים.

items.label: Poem
items.title: רחל בלובשטיין — רק על עצמי
items.summary:
לָמָּה קְרָאתֶם לִי, חוֹפֵי הַפֶּלֶא?
לָמָּה כְּזַבְתֶּם, אוֹרוֹת רְחוֹקִים?

items.label: Poem
items.title: שאול טשרניחובסקי — אומרים: ישנה ארץ
items.summary:
אוֹמְרִים: יֶשְׁנָהּ אֶרֶץ,
אֶרֶץ שְׁכוּרַת שֶׁמֶשׁ – – –
אַיֵּה אוֹתָהּ אֶרֶץ,
אַיֵּה אוֹתָהּ שֶׁמֶשׁ?

items.label: Poem
items.title: שאול טשרניחובסקי — אומרים: ישנה ארץ
items.summary:
יֶשְׁנָהּ אֶרֶץ,
עַמּוּדֶיהָ שִׁבְעָה,
שִׁבְעָה כוֹכְבֵי-לֶכֶת
צָצִים עַל כָּל גִּבְעָה.

items.label: Poem
items.title: שאול טשרניחובסקי — אומרים: ישנה ארץ
items.summary:
אֶרֶץ –
בָּהּ יִתְקַיֵּם
כָּל אֲשֶׁר אִישׁ קִוָּה –
אֵיפֹה הִיא הָאָרֶץ?
אַיֵּה אוֹתָהּ גִּבְעָה?

items.label: Poem
items.title: שאול טשרניחובסקי — אומרים: ישנה ארץ
items.summary:
נִכְנַס
כָּל הַנִּכְנָס,
פָּגַע בְּאָח כְּהִגָּמְלוֹ,
פּוֹרֵשׂ אֵלָיו שָׁלוֹם –
וְאוֹר לָאִישׁ וְחָם לוֹ.

items.label: Poem
items.title: יהודה הלוי — שובי נפשי למנוחיכי
items.summary:
שׁוּבִי, נַפְשִׁי לִמְנוּחָיְכִי
כִּי יְיָ גָּמַל עָלָיְכִי!
יְקָרָה, מִיְּקָר יוֹצְרֵךְ לְקוּחָה,
קוּמִי, כִּי לֹא זֹאת הַמְּנוּחָה!

items.label: Poem
items.title: יהודה הלוי — שובי נפשי למנוחיכי
items.summary:
הָאֹרַח רַב, קְחִי לָךְ אֲרוּחָה –
עֵת לַעֲשׂוֹת חֵפֶץ עוֹשָׂיְכִי!
הִנֵּה אֲנִי תוֹשָׁב כְּכָל‑אֲבוֹתָי
וּכְצֵל עוֹבֵר יֶתֶר שְׁנוֹתָי –

items.label: Poem
items.title: יהודה הלוי — לבי במזרח
items.summary:
לִבִּי בְמִזְרָח וְאָנֹכִי בְּסוֹף מַעֲרָב
אֵיךְ אֶטְעֲמָה אֵת אֲשֶׁר אֹכַל וְאֵיךְ יֶעֱרָב
אֵיכָה אֲשַׁלֵּם נְדָרַי וָאֱסָרַי, בְּעוֹד
צִיּוֹן בְּחֶבֶל אֱדוֹם וַאֲנִי בְּכֶבֶל עֲרָב
יֵקַל בְּעֵינַי עֲזֹב כָּל טוּב סְפָרַד, כְּמוֹ
יֵקַר בְּעֵינַי רְאוֹת עַפְרוֹת דְּבִיר נֶחֱרָב.

items.label: Poem
items.title: יהודה הלוי — שער שיבה בהראות יחידי
items.summary:
שְׂעַר שֵׂיבָה בְּהֵרָאוֹת יְחִידִי
עֲלֵי רֹאשִי קְטַפְטִיהוּ בְיָדִי
הֳשִׁיבַנִי יְכָלְתּנִי לְבַדִּי
וּמַה תַּעְשֶׂה בְּבֹא אַחֲרַי גְּדוּדִי.
